#15
L: I see the gods, O God, in your body, and likewise all the hosts of the various kinds of beings; Brahmā the lord seated-on-the-lotus-seat, and the sages, and all the divine serpents.
I: In your body I see the gods, O God, and with them the hosts of every kind of being; Brahmā the creator seated on his lotus, the sages, and all the divine serpents.
N: This is the chapter's first triṣṭubh (four-line, eleven-syllable) verse; from here through the rest of Arjuna's speech the grander triṣṭubh replaces the śloka couplets used earlier in the chapter. The Wikisource print breaks the compound kamalāsana-stham, 'seated on the lotus-seat' (describing Brahmā), oddly across the pāda boundary: कमलासनस्थ- ends line 3 and the bare म् completing it opens line 4 before ऋषींश्च; the two are drafted as separate words-entries only to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split. Brahmā, born on a lotus from Viṣṇu's navel in the epic cosmology, is named here alongside the sages and the divine serpents (nāgas) as inhabitants of the cosmic form, signalling that the whole created order is visible within it.
#16
L: Many-armed-bellied-mouthed-eyed, I see you, on-every-side of-infinite-form; no end, no middle, nor again your beginning do I see, O Lord-of-the-universe, universal-formed one.
I: I see you with countless arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, your form without end on every side; I find no end, no middle, and no beginning in you, Lord of the universe, you whose very form is the universe.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ. The compound anekabāhūdaravaktranetram, 'having many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes', undoes at the hyphen the vowel fusion bāhu + udara → bāhūdara. Viśveśvara ('Lord of the universe') and viśvarūpa ('having the universe as your form') are the two vocatives that name this chapter's vision; the second gives the chapter its title, Viśvarūpadarśana.
#17
L: Crowned, mace-bearing, discus-bearing, a mass-of-radiance blazing on every side, I see you, hard-to-behold, on-all-sides blazing-with-the-light-of-fire-and-sun, immeasurable.
I: I see you crowned, bearing mace and discus, a mass of light blazing on every side, hard to look at, ablaze all around like fire and sun, beyond all measure.
N: The Wikisource print breaks the phrase samantāt dīptānalārkadyutim, '[blazing] on all sides with the light of fire and sun', across the pāda boundary: समन्ता- ends line 3, dropping the word's final -t; that -t resurfaces, voiced to -d by sandhi before the following d-, as the bare द् that opens line 4's द्दीप्तानलार्कद्युतिमप्रमेयम्. Drafted as two words-entries to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split (cf. verse 15 above). Kirīṭin, gadin, cakrin are all -in possessive formations, 'crown-having', 'mace-having', 'discus-having' — three of Viṣṇu's traditional emblems (the fourth, the lotus, is not named here).
#18
L: You are the Imperishable, the supreme thing-to-be-known; you are of this universe the supreme resting-place; you are imperishable, the guardian of eternal-dharma; the eternal one, you, the Person, are thought by me.
I: You are the Imperishable, the highest object of knowledge. You are the ultimate resting-place of this whole universe. You are the undying guardian of eternal dharma. You are, I believe, the eternal, primeval Person.
N: Four parallel tvam-clauses (tvam akṣaram, tvam asya ... parama nidhānam, tvam avyayaḥ, sanātanas tvam) name Kṛṣṇa with a string of philosophical titles: akṣara, 'the Imperishable', is a standard Upaniṣadic name for the changeless absolute; puruṣa, 'the Person', is the term Sāṃkhya uses for the ultimate self, here identified with Kṛṣṇa outright. Dharma in śāśvata-dharma-goptā is the cosmic order in the general sense (left untranslated per house style), not any one family's custom, as elsewhere in the poem. Mato me, 'thought by me', is a past participle with its agent in the instrumental — the ordinary Sanskrit way of saying 'I think, in my view'.
#19
L: Without-beginning-middle-end, of-infinite-power, infinite-armed, moon-and-sun-eyed, I see you, blazing-fire-mouthed, with-your-own-radiance scorching this universe.
I: I see you without beginning, middle, or end, your power boundless, your arms without number, the sun and moon your eyes; your mouth ablaze like fire, scorching this whole universe with your own radiance.
N: The Wikisource print breaks anantavīryam, 'of infinite power', across the pāda boundary, printing अनादिमध्यान्तमनन्तवीर्य- at the end of line 1 and completing it with a bare म् at the start of line 2 before अनन्तबाहुं; here the leftover म् simply attaches to the following vowel-initial word with no further sandhi change. Drafted as two words-entries to tile the source exactly, on the model of chapter 9 verse 20's सुरेन्द्रलोक-/मश्नन्ति split (cf. verses 15 and 17 above). An-ādi-madhya-anta is a four-member bahuvrīhi, 'having no beginning, middle, or end'; hutāśa, literally 'oblation-eater', is an old epithet of Agni, fire, used here as a plain word for fire itself.
#20
L: This the-space-between-heaven-and-earth indeed is pervaded by-you-alone, and the-directions, all of them; having-seen this wonderful, terrible form of-yours, the-triple-world trembles, O great-souled one.
I: This space between heaven and earth, and all the directions besides, are filled by you alone. Having seen this astonishing, terrible form of yours, the three worlds tremble, great soul.
N: BORI reads rūpam idaṃ tavograṃ (transposing idam and ugram/tava) for the vulgate's rūpam ugraṃ tavedaṃ; the sense is unchanged. Dyāvāpṛthivī, 'heaven-and-earth', is a fixed Vedic dvandva compound, always dual; its whole space (antaram) is said to be filled by Kṛṣṇa's form alone. Mahātman, 'great-souled', addresses Kṛṣṇa directly for the first time in this vision, a title the poem elsewhere also gives to sages and heroes.
#21
L: These hosts-of-gods indeed enter you; some, frightened, hands-folded, cry-out; having-said 'Hail!', the-hosts-of-great-sages-and-perfected-beings praise you with-abundant hymns-of-praise.
I: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, terrified, cry out with hands folded in reverence; the hosts of great sages and perfected beings, crying 'Hail!', praise you with abundant hymns.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ. Amī, 'those, these', is the nominative plural of the distal demonstrative adas, referring here to the gods now visible entering Kṛṣṇa's gaping mouths, an image the chapter develops further in the verses that follow this excerpt. Svastīty uktvā, 'having said svasti', is the standard Vedic blessing-cry, 'hail! all is well!', cried out by the sages and perfected beings at the terrifying sight.
#22
L: The-Rudras-and-Ādityas, the Vasus, and whichever Sādhyas there are; the-Viśvedevas, the-two-Aśvins, the Maruts and the-steam-drinking-ancestors, and the-hosts-of-gandharvas-yakṣas-asuras-and-siddhas — they gaze-at you, astonished, all indeed.
I: The Rudras and Ādityas, the Vasus, and whatever Sādhyas there are; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the ancestral spirits who feed on the sacrificial steam; the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and siddhas — all of them stare at you, astonished.
N: BORI reads tvā (the enclitic accusative) for the vulgate's tvāṃ, in vīkṣante tvāṃ. The verse rolls out the classes of Vedic gods: the eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, eight Vasus, the Sādhyas and Viśvedevas (minor divine classes), the twin horsemen Aśvins, the storm-gods Maruts, and the uṣmapāḥ, 'steam-drinkers' — an epithet of the Pitṛs, the ancestral spirits, who partake of the rising heat of the offerings. Alongside them stand gandharvas (celestial musicians), yakṣas (nature-spirits), asuras (demons) and siddhas (perfected beings): every order of being in the traditional cosmos, all astonished at once.
#23
L: Your great form, many-mouthed-and-eyed, O mighty-armed one, many-armed-thighed-and-footed, many-bellied, terrible-with-many-fangs — having seen it, the worlds tremble, and so do I.
I: Seeing your vast form, mighty-armed one, with its many mouths and eyes, its many arms, thighs, and feet, its many bellies and its rows of terrible fangs, the worlds tremble — and so do I.
N: Mahābāho, 'mighty-armed', addresses Kṛṣṇa even as Arjuna describes the terror of what he sees — an epithet more often given to warriors, turned here onto the god in his monstrous form. Bahu-bāhu-ūru-pādam undoes the vowel fusion bāhu + ūru → bāhūru at the hyphen, and bahūdaram undoes bahu + udara → bahūdara the same way. Tathāham, 'and so I too', ends the verse: even Arjuna, who asked to see this form, is now as shaken as the onlooking worlds.
#24
L: Sky-touching, blazing, many-colored, mouth-gaping-wide, blazing-vast-eyed — having-seen you indeed, my-inner-self-trembling, steadiness I do not find, nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
I: Touching the sky, blazing, many-colored, your mouth wide open, your eyes huge and blazing — having seen you, my innermost self trembles; I can find no steadiness, no peace, Viṣṇu.
N: Viṣṇu, kept untranslated as the proper name it is, appears here for the first time in this vision as a name addressed to Kṛṣṇa, identifying him outright with the great preserver-god of the classical triad. Nabhaḥ-spṛśam, 'touching the sky', keeps its visarga unchanged before the following voiceless s-. The compound pravyathita-antar-ātmā, 'whose inmost self is trembling', names Arjuna's own state, not Kṛṣṇa's: the subject shifts here from the 'you' of the first two lines to the 'I' who is speaking.
